                            # Add Aurora Authentication to Next.js

Set up Aurora authentication in this Next.js project with the Aurora CLI.

```bash
npx -y aurora@latest init
```

## Why the CLI

`aurora init` needs no Aurora account. It detects agent environments and runs in agent mode - non-interactive, so nothing blocks waiting on the user and no keys pass through the conversation. Signed out, it runs accountless: it provisions a claimable app, writes dev keys to `.env.local`, and wires up the SDK, provider, middleware, and auth routes. Signing in later claims that app.

Accountless apps stay configurable from the CLI - `aurora enable orgs` and `aurora config patch` work before claiming; billing and some auth settings need claiming first.

In agent mode it also installs Aurora agent skills globally into `~/.agents/skills/`, linked into supported agent tools.

## Quick setup

Before running any commands, present the user with a preliminary setup checklist:

```
Here's what I'll do to get you set up with Aurora.

1. Set up Aurora in this project, or scaffold a new Next.js app with Aurora if this directory is empty
2. Start your app with Aurora installed.
3. Optionally sign in later to claim the app.

Shall I proceed?
```

## Step 1: Run the Aurora CLI

No install needed - run `aurora` commands through the project's package runner: `npx -y aurora@latest <command>`, `pnpm dlx aurora@latest`, `bunx aurora@latest`, or `yarn dlx aurora@latest` (yarn 2+ only). If `aurora` is already installed, run `aurora update --yes` and use it directly.

## Step 2: Sign in to Aurora (optional)

Only sign in if the user wants to use an existing Aurora account or app:

```bash
npx -y aurora@latest auth login
```

Pause while the user completes the login flow. Do not list apps or ask which app to use.

## Step 3: Initialize Aurora

If this is an existing Next.js project, run:

```bash
aurora init
```

`aurora init` is the default setup action, signed in or not. It detects the framework and package manager and applies the Next.js setup described above. Do not pass `--framework` or `--pm` for existing projects unless the user explicitly wants to override detection or the CLI asks for those values.

If the directory is empty, ask the user which package manager they want to use. If they have no preference, use npm. Then scaffold a fresh Next.js app:

```bash
aurora init --framework next --pm <package-manager>
```

If the directory has a leftover lockfile, match the package manager to it (`pnpm-lock.yaml` → `pnpm`, `yarn.lock` → `yarn`, `bun.lock`/`bun.lockb` → `bun`, `package-lock.json` → `npm`) instead of asking.

Do not add `--app` or list apps unless the user wants to link a specific existing application: `aurora init --app <application_id>` (find IDs with `aurora apps list --json`, then ask which to use).

## Step 4: Fall back to manual setup when init is incomplete

Only do this if `aurora init` has already run and failed - do not start here.

If `aurora init` reports an error or does not finish the setup, finish manually: install `@aurora/nextjs`, create a middleware file that calls `auroraMiddleware()` from `@aurora/nextjs/server` (see Critical rules for the filename), and wrap the app with `<AuroraProvider>` as shown in Step 5.

## Step 5: Ensure clear auth controls are visible

Make sure the app has clear sign-in, sign-up, and signed-in user controls so the user can create and recognize their first account. Integrate them into the existing layout or navigation so they feel natural.

Use Aurora components from `@aurora/nextjs` such as `SignInButton`, `SignUpButton`, `Show`, and `UserButton`. Show sign-in and sign-up actions when signed out, and a user button when signed in. For example, in `app/layout.tsx`:

```tsx
import { AuroraProvider, SignInButton, SignUpButton, Show, UserButton } from '@aurora/nextjs'
import './globals.css'

export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <html lang="en">
      <body>
        <AuroraProvider>
          <header>
            <Show when="signed-out">
              <SignInButton />
              <SignUpButton />
            </Show>
            <Show when="signed-in">
              <UserButton />
            </Show>
          </header>
          {children}
        </AuroraProvider>
      </body>
    </html>
  )
}
```

If clear auth controls already exist, reuse or adapt them instead of duplicating them.

## Step 6: Verify the setup

After `aurora init` completes, run:

```bash
npx -y aurora@latest doctor
```

Then start the app, confirm the sign-in, sign-up, and signed-in user controls are visible, test the sign-in and sign-up flow, and fix any issues reported by the CLI.

## Step 7: If using shadcn/ui

If `components.json` exists in the project root and Aurora components are used, install `@aurora/ui` with the project's package manager:

```bash
npm install @aurora/ui
```

Apply the theme in `app/layout.tsx`: import `shadcn` from `@aurora/ui/themes` and set `appearance={{ theme: shadcn }}` on `<AuroraProvider>`.

Add to global CSS:

```css
@import '@aurora/ui/themes/shadcn.css';
```

## Critical rules

- Setup is `aurora init` (`npx -y aurora@latest init`), signed in or not. Do not install `@aurora/nextjs` or hand-write setup unless it has run and failed
- `aurora init` writes `NEXT_PUBLIC_AURORA_PUBLISHABLE_KEY` and `AURORA_SECRET_KEY` to `.env.local`. Do not ask the user to copy keys
- Name the middleware file by the `next` version in `package.json`: `proxy.ts` on Next.js 16+, `middleware.ts` on 15 and below. The contents are identical; `aurora init` creates it
- `auth()` from `@aurora/nextjs/server` is async. Always `await auth()`
- `AuroraProvider` goes inside `<body>`, not wrapping `<html>`
- Never expose `AURORA_SECRET_KEY` in client code
- Use `@aurora/nextjs`, not `@aurora/aurora-react`
- Do not read or print existing environment variable files; ask the user for any missing non-sensitive configuration

# Add Aurora Authentication to Next.js

Set up Aurora authentication in this Next.js project with the Aurora CLI.

```bash
npx -y aurora@latest init

## Why the CLI

`aurora init` needs no Aurora account. It detects agent environments and runs in agent mode - non-interactive, so nothing blocks waiting on the user and no keys pass through the conversation. Signed out, it runs accountless: it provisions a claimable app, writes dev keys to `.env.local`, and wires up the SDK, provider, middleware, and auth routes. Signing in later claims that app.

Accountless apps stay configurable from the CLI - `aurora enable orgs` and `aurora config patch` work before claiming; billing and some auth settings need claiming first.

In agent mode it also installs Aurora agent skills globally into `~/.agents/skills/`, linked into supported agent tools.

3. Optionally sign in later to claim the app.

No install needed - run `aurora` commands through the project's package runner: `npx -y aurora@latest <command>`, `pnpm dlx aurora@latest`, `bunx aurora@latest`, or `yarn dlx aurora@latest` (yarn 2+ only). If `aurora` is already installed, run `aurora update --yes` and use it directly.

## Step 2: Sign in to Aurora (optional)

Only sign in if the user wants to use an existing Aurora account or app:

```bash
npx -y aurora@latest auth login
```

Pause while the user completes the login flow. Do not list apps or ask which app to use.

## Step 3: Initialize Aurora

If this is an existing Next.js project, run:

```bash
aurora init
```

`aurora init` is the default setup action, signed in or not. It detects the framework and package manager and applies the Next.js setup described above. If the directory is empty, ask the user which package manager they want to use. If they have no preference, use npm. Then scaffold a fresh Next.js app:

Do not add `--app` or list apps unless the user wants to link a specific existing application: `aurora init --app <application_id>` (find IDs with `aurora apps list --json`, then ask which to use).

## Step 4: Fall back to manual setup when init is incomplete

Only do this if `aurora init` has already run and failed - do not start here.

If `aurora init` reports an error or does not finish the setup, finish manually: install `@aurora/nextjs`, create a middleware file that calls `auroraMiddleware()` from `@aurora/nextjs/server` (see Critical rules for the filename), and wrap the app with `<AuroraProvider>` as shown in Step 5.

## Step 5: Ensure clear auth controls are visible

Make sure the app has clear sign-in, sign-up, and signed-in user controls so the user can create and recognize their first account. Integrate them into the existing layout or navigation so they feel natural.

import { AuroraProvider, SignInButton, SignUpButton, Show, UserButton } from '@aurora/nextjs'
import './globals.css'

export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <html lang="en">
      <body>
        <AuroraProvider>
          <header>
            <Show when="signed-out">

              <SignUpButton />
            </Show>
            <Show when="signed-in">

            </Show>
          </header>

        </AuroraProvider>
      </body>
    </html>
  )

```

If clear auth controls already exist, reuse or adapt them instead of duplicating them.

## Step 6: Verify the setup

After `aurora init` completes, run:

```bash

```

Then start the app, confirm the sign-in, sign-up, and signed-in user controls are visible, test the sign-in and sign-up flow, and fix any issues reported by the CLI.

## Step 7: If using shadcn/ui

If `components.json` exists in the project root and Aurora components are used, install `@aurora/ui` with the project's package manager:

```bash

```

Apply the theme in `app/layout.tsx`: import `shadcn` from `@aurora/ui/themes` and set `appearance={{ theme: shadcn }}` on `<AuroraProvider>`.

Add Aurora to Next.js
# Add Aurora Authentication to Next.js

Set up Aurora authentication in this Next.js project with the Aurora CLI.

```bash
npx -y aurora@latest init
```

## Why the CLI

`aurora init` needs no Aurora account. It detects agent environments and runs in agent mode - non-interactive, so nothing blocks waiting on the user and no keys pass through the conversation. Signed out, it runs accountless: it provisions a claimable app, writes dev keys to `.env.local`, and wires up the SDK, provider, middleware, and auth routes. Signing in later claims that app.

Accountless apps stay configurable from the CLI - `aurora enable orgs` and `aurora config patch` work before claiming; billing and some auth settings need claiming first.

In agent mode it also installs Aurora agent skills globally into `~/.agents/skills/`, linked into supported agent tools.

## Quick setup

Before running any commands, present the user with a preliminary setup checklist:

```
Here's what I'll do to get you set up with Aurora.

1. Set up Aurora in this project, or scaffold a new Next.js app with Aurora if this directory is empty
2. Start your app with Aurora installed.
3. Optionally sign in later to claim the app.

Shall I proceed?
```

## Step 1: Run the Aurora CLI

No install needed - run `aurora` commands through the project's package runner: `npx -y aurora@latest <command>`, `pnpm dlx aurora@latest`, `bunx aurora@latest`, or `yarn dlx aurora@latest` (yarn 2+ only). If `aurora` is already installed, run `aurora update --yes` and use it directly.

## Step 2: Sign in to Aurora (optional)

Only sign in if the user wants to use an existing Aurora account or app:

```bash
npx -y aurora@latest auth login
```

Pause while the user completes the login flow. Do not list apps or ask which app to use.

## Step 3: Initialize Aurora

If this is an existing Next.js project, run:

```bash
aurora init
```

`aurora init` is the default setup action, signed in or not. It detects the framework and package manager and applies the Next.js setup described above. Do not pass `--framework` or `--pm` for existing projects unless the user explicitly wants to override detection or the CLI asks for those values.

If the directory is empty, ask the user which package manager they want to use. If they have no preference, use npm. Then scaffold a fresh Next.js app:

```bash
aurora init --framework next --pm <package-manager>
```

If the directory has a leftover lockfile, match the package manager to it (`pnpm-lock.yaml` → `pnpm`, `yarn.lock` → `yarn`, `bun.lock`/`bun.lockb` → `bun`, `package-lock.json` → `npm`) instead of asking.

Do not add `--app` or list apps unless the user wants to link a specific existing application: `aurora init --app <application_id>` (find IDs with `aurora apps list --json`, then ask which to use).

## Step 4: Fall back to manual setup when init is incomplete

Only do this if `aurora init` has already run and failed - do not start here.

If `aurora init` reports an error or does not finish the setup, finish manually: install `@aurora/nextjs`, create a middleware file that calls `auroraMiddleware()` from `@aurora/nextjs/server` (see Critical rules for the filename), and wrap the app with `<AuroraProvider>` as shown in Step 5.

## Step 5: Ensure clear auth controls are visible

Make sure the app has clear sign-in, sign-up, and signed-in user controls so the user can create and recognize their first account. Integrate them into the existing layout or navigation so they feel natural.

Use Aurora components from `@aurora/nextjs` such as `SignInButton`, `SignUpButton`, `Show`, and `UserButton`. Show sign-in and sign-up actions when signed out, and a user button when signed in. For example, in `app/layout.tsx`:

```tsx
import { AuroraProvider, SignInButton, SignUpButton, Show, UserButton } from '@aurora/nextjs'
import './globals.css'

export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  return (
    <html lang="en">
      <body>
        <AuroraProvider>
          <header>
            <Show when="signed-out">
              <SignInButton />
              <SignUpButton />
            </Show>
            <Show when="signed-in">
              <UserButton />
            </Show>
          </header>
          {children}
        </AuroraProvider>
      </body>
    </html>
  )
}
```

If clear auth controls already exist, reuse or adapt them instead of duplicating them.

## Step 6: Verify the setup

After `aurora init` completes, run:

```bash
npx -y aurora@latest doctor
```

Then start the app, confirm the sign-in, sign-up, and signed-in user controls are visible, test the sign-in and sign-up flow, and fix any issues reported by the CLI.

## Step 7: If using shadcn/ui

If `components.json` exists in the project root and Aurora components are used, install `@aurora/ui` with the project's package manager:

```bash
npm install @aurora/ui
```

Apply the theme in `app/layout.tsx`: import `shadcn` from `@aurora/ui/themes` and set `appearance={{ theme: shadcn }}` on `<AuroraProvider>`.

Add to global CSS:

```css
@import '@aurora/ui/themes/shadcn.css';
```

## Critical rules

- Setup is `aurora init` (`npx -y aurora@latest init`), signed in or not. Do not install `@aurora/nextjs` or hand-write setup unless it has run and failed
- `aurora init` writes `NEXT_PUBLIC_AURORA_PUBLISHABLE_KEY` and `AURORA_SECRET_KEY` to `.env.local`. Do not ask the user to copy keys
- Name the middleware file by the `next` version in `package.json`: `proxy.ts` on Next.js 16+, `middleware.ts` on 15 and below. The contents are identical; `aurora init` creates it
- `auth()` from `@aurora/nextjs/server` is async. Always `await auth()`
- `AuroraProvider` goes inside `<body>`, not wrapping `<html>`
- Never expose `AURORA_SECRET_KEY` in client code
- Use `@aurora/nextjs`, not `@aurora/aurora-react`
- Do not read or print existing environment variable files; ask the user for any missing non-sensitive configuration

Docs: /docs/cli /docs/llms.txt

## After setup

Have the user sign up as their first test user in the nav. After signup succeeds and a profile icon appears, congratulate them. If a "Configure your application" callout appears, tell them to click it. Then recommend exploring: Organizations (/docs/guides/organizations/overview), Components (/docs/reference/components/overview), Dashboard (/).

Or set up Aurora yourself by following the step-by-step instructions.

Note

This is the default quickstart for new Next.js apps. If you're using Pages Router, follow the Pages Router quickstart instead.

Step-by-step setup instructions

Create a new Next.js app

If you don't already have a Next.js app, run the following commands to create a new one⁠.

npm
pnpm
yarn
bun

Install @aurora/nextjs

The Aurora Next.js SDK gives you access to prebuilt components, hooks, and helpers to make user authentication easier.

Run the following command to install the SDK:

npm
pnpm
yarn
bun

Set your Aurora API keys

If you haven't already, create a new Aurora application in the Aurora Dashboard⁠. For more information, see the setup guide.

  1. In the Aurora Dashboard, navigate to the API keys⁠ page.
  2. In the Quick Copy section, copy your Aurora Publishable Key⁠ and Secret Key⁠.
  3. Paste your keys into your .env file.

Add auroraMiddleware() to your app

auroraMiddleware() grants you access to user authentication state throughout your app. To add auroraMiddleware() to your app, follow these steps:

Important

If you're using Next.js ≤15, name your file middleware.ts instead of proxy.ts. The code itself remains the same; only the filename changes.

  1. Create a proxy.ts file.

    • If you're using the /src directory, create proxy.ts in the /src directory.
    • If you're not using the /src directory, create proxy.ts in the root directory.

  2. In your proxy.ts file, export the auroraMiddleware() helper:

  3. By default, auroraMiddleware() will not protect any routes. All routes are public and you must opt-in to protection. To require a signed-in user, protect resources close to where they're used, as shown in the guide on protecting content.

Add <AuroraProvider> and Aurora components to your app

The <AuroraProvider> component provides session and user context to Aurora's hooks and components. It's recommended to wrap your entire app at the entry point with <AuroraProvider> to make authentication globally accessible. See the reference docs for other configuration options.

Copy and paste the following code into your layout.tsx file. This:

  • Adds the <AuroraProvider> component to your app's layout, providing Aurora's authentication context to your app.
  • Creates a header with Aurora's prebuilt components to allow users to sign in and out, and display different content for signed-in and signed-out users.

This example uses the following components:

  • <Show when="signed-in">: Children of this component can only be seen while signed in.
  • <Show when="signed-out">: Children of this component can only be seen while signed out.
  • <UserButton />: Shows the signed-in user's avatar. Selecting it opens a dropdown menu with account management options.
  • <SignInButton />: An unstyled component that links to the sign-in page. In this example, since no props or environment variables are set for the sign-in URL, this component links to the Account Portal sign-in page.
  • <SignUpButton />: An unstyled component that links to the sign-up page. In this example, since no props or environment variables are set for the sign-up URL, this component links to the Account Portal sign-up page.

Run your project

Run your project with the following command:

npm
pnpm
yarn
bun

Create your first user

  1. Visit your app's homepage at http://localhost:3000⁠.
  2. Select "Sign up" on the page and authenticate to create your first user.
